title: Video: Dexterous robot hand learns the delicate art of silk embroidery
key_facts: Agilink, a spin-off of Chinese robotics company AgiBot, trained its OmniHand 3 Ultra robot hand with Suzhou embroidery master Fu Xianghong.
The hand learned to split silk strands, thread a needle, stretch fabric across a frame and stitch.
Splitting the thread means one finger teases apart the strands (16, per the video) while the others hold tension.
The model in the video is not named; it looks identical to the OmniHand 3 Ultra-M, about human-hand size, 630 g, direct-drive, holds 3 kg stably, repeats positions to about 0.2 mm.
Fingertip vision-based sensors measure force in three dimensions and detect deformations of 0.08 mm, per the company.
New Atlas says fine force control is a bottleneck for humanoids, and such hands could matter most in homes rather than most factory jobs.
quote_evidence: Agilink, a spin-off of Chinese robotics giant AgiBot, asked Fu Xianghong, a master of traditional Suzhou embroidery, to train its OmniHand 3 Ultra.
The synthetic hand has learned to split silk strands, thread a needle, stretch fabric across a frame, and stitch.
Agilink hasn't said exactly which model appears in the video.
why_it_matters_hint: Fine touch and force control is a bottleneck for humanoid robots working safely around people.
notes: Company video and claims; no independent test. Model in video not confirmed by Agilink.
